name: Morton's neuroma
aka: common plantar digital nerve perineural fibrosis
populations: middle-aged women (female:male about 5:1 in one review)
people who wear tight, narrow or high-heeled footwear (proposed)
runners and dancers with high forefoot loading (clinical observation)
adults referred to foot and ankle surgeons with forefoot pain
summary: Perineural fibrosis of a common plantar digital nerve, most often in the 3rd web space, causing burning forefoot pain and a pebble-in-the-shoe feeling. The evidence for injection and surgery is limited and mixed.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Variable. In one review, footwear changes and orthoses gave convincing results only within about 4.5 months and for neuromas smaller than 5–6 mm; surgery is considered when nonoperative care fails

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: No validated criteria. Return as forefoot loading is tolerated in suitable footwear; after surgery, follow the surgeon's protocol (clinical convention)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Web space tenderness with a squeeze: the modified thumb–index finger squeeze test had sensitivity 0.96 and LR– 0.04 in one study; patient-reported clicking was specific (0.96)

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Often not needed. In one series, clinical diagnosis had 98% sensitivity, ultrasound 90% and MRI 88%; up to 25% of people have asymptomatic neuroma-like findings

keyFacts.label: Pathology
keyFacts.value: Benign perineural fibrosis of a common plantar digital nerve, usually in the third intermetatarsal space; it is not a true neoplasm

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: 87.5 versus 50.2 cases per 100 000 UK females versus males; third web space affected in 43–86% of neuromas

overview:
Morton's neuroma is a painful condition of a common plantar digital nerve in the forefoot, occurring most often in the third web space and less often in the second [r1]. Despite the name it is not a true neoplasm. The histological endpoint is benign perineural fibrosis of the nerve [r2,r3]. Typical symptoms are burning or shooting pain in the web space that extends to the toes, or the sensation of walking on a pebble, which limit weightbearing activities and quality of life [r1].

Diagnosis is mainly clinical, but the accuracy of individual tests is modest. In a systematic review, patient-reported clicking was the only strong rule-in feature, and Mulder's sign, the foot squeeze test and web space tenderness gave only weak evidence [r4]. Imaging is useful when the picture is unclear or several web spaces are involved, and neuroma-like findings are common in people without symptoms [r5,r6]. Treatment is stepwise. The Cochrane review found only six small randomised trials, with low to moderate certainty: adding corticosteroid to local anaesthetic made little difference to pain or function, while ultrasound-guided injection probably performed better than non-guided injection [r1]. Surgical outcomes range from 89.4% good results at a median of 7.1 years to 61% satisfaction at more than 10 years [r7,r8]. The Cochrane review included no trial comparing surgery with nonoperative care [r1].

epidemiology.text: Morton's neuroma has been reported in all four intermetatarsal spaces. The third space is most often affected (reported range 43–86.4% of neuromas), followed by the second (5.1–57%). It is more common in females (87.5 versus 50.2 cases per 100 000 of the UK population) and is the third most common condition referred to UK foot and ankle surgeons [r4]. A systematic review of injection therapy states that it affects about 4% of the general population [r9]; the two figures measure different things and should not be compared directly. A review of conservative treatment reports a female-to-male ratio of 5:1 and an average age of 50 years at surgery [r10]. Imaging studies find neuroma-like lesions in up to 25% of people without symptoms [r6]. In a retrospective series of 43 excised neuromas, tenderness on direct palpation was present in 100%, pain on weightbearing in 91% and relief with rest in 81% [r5].

intrinsic: Anatomy of the web space: the common plantar digital nerve runs beneath the deep transverse intermetatarsal ligament (standard anatomy), where it can be compressed or tethered (the entrapment theory) [r3]
Forefoot biomechanics: a role for biomechanics is proposed in the development of the condition, but specific foot types were not tested in the sources reviewed [r10]

Toe divergence on weightbearing radiographs (the 'Vulcan salute' sign) was present in 30 of 100 patients with MRI-proven neuroma versus 3 of 100 controls, but whether it is a cause or a consequence is unknown [r11]
extrinsic: Tight, narrow or high-heeled footwear that squeezes the forefoot. A narrative review suggests that long, broad-toed, flat-heeled shoes with a reasonably stiff sole may prevent or delay the condition, but no controlled evidence was identified [r10]
Repetitive forefoot loading with the toes extended, for example in running, dance, squatting and kneeling (proposed under the repetitive trauma theory; clinical observation) [r3]
Previous forefoot surgery or neurectomy, which can leave a recurrent (stump) neuroma [r12]
Prolonged standing and walking on hard surfaces in unsuitable footwear (clinical observation; not tested)

mechanism.summary: There is no single injury. Four theories are cited: chronic repetitive trauma, ischaemia, entrapment of the nerve beneath the deep transverse intermetatarsal ligament, and intermetatarsal bursitis [r3,r10]. The common pathway proposed is repeated compression and traction of a common plantar digital nerve in the web space, particularly when the forefoot is squeezed in tight footwear or the toes are extended at push-off. The nerve then develops perineural fibrosis, which makes it thicker and easier to pinch [r3,r2]. The cause remains controversial [r2].
sequence: The forefoot is loaded repeatedly with the toes extended: push-off in running and dance, high heels, or narrow shoes that squeeze the metatarsal heads together [r3,r10].

In the third web space, the common plantar digital nerve passes beneath the deep transverse intermetatarsal ligament (standard anatomy), so the metatarsal heads and the ligament can compress it from above and below [r3].
Repeated compression, traction and microtrauma, possibly with local ischaemia and an inflamed intermetatarsal bursa, irritate the nerve [r3].
Over months the nerve develops degeneration, perineural fibrosis, arterial degeneration and oedema of the endoneurium [r4].
The thickened nerve is pinched more easily and becomes mechanically sensitive (clinical reasoning).
The patient has burning, shooting or electric pain in the web space that extends to the toes, a sensation of a pebble in the shoe, and relief with rest and with removing the shoe [r1,r5].
Squeezing the forefoot while pressing the web space can displace the thickened tissue and produce a click, known as Mulder's click (a sign of limited and variable accuracy) [r4].

variants.name: Third web space neuroma (classic)
variants.description: The most common site: reported in 43–86.4% of neuromas [r4]. Pain is felt between the third and fourth toes [r1].

variants.name: Second web space neuroma
variants.description: Less common, reported in 5.1–57% of neuromas [r4]. Among 25 recurrent neuromas in one series, 44% were in the second web space and 56% in the third [r12].

variants.name: Multiple web spaces
variants.description: More than one affected space is one of two indications for imaging in one retrospective series [r5]. Consider other causes of forefoot pain if several spaces are affected.

variants.name: Recurrent (stump) neuroma after neurectomy
variants.description: Recurrent symptoms after neurectomy can be due to a recurrent neuroma, which can be diagnosed clinically and with ultrasound; the reported success rate after excision of a primary neuroma is 74% [r12].

variants.name: Neuroma-like lesions from other causes
variants.description: A plantar plate rupture can be associated with a neuroma-like mass in the intermetatarsal space, and rheumatoid or gouty nodules, intermetatarsal bursitis and tenosynovial giant cell tumour can look similar on MRI [r6].

anatomy.text: The common plantar digital nerves arise from the medial and lateral plantar nerves, run through the intermetatarsal spaces and divide into proper digital nerves to the adjacent sides of two toes. In the web space the nerve lies plantar to the deep transverse metatarsal ligament, with an intermetatarsal bursa and the digital vessels (standard anatomy; the anatomy is reviewed in [r2]). The third common plantar digital nerve is the one most often affected [r4]. The histological endpoint of Morton's neuroma is perineural fibrosis of a common plantar digital nerve, usually in the third intermetatarsal space [r2].

structures.name: Third common plantar digital nerve
structures.role: Sensory nerve to the adjacent sides of the third and fourth toes; the most frequent site of perineural fibrosis [r2,r4]

structures.name: Second common plantar digital nerve
structures.role: Sensory nerve to the adjacent sides of the second and third toes; the second most frequent site [r4]

structures.name: Deep transverse intermetatarsal ligament
structures.role: Joins the plantar plates and metatarsal heads; the nerve passes beneath it, so it is the proposed site of entrapment [r3,r2]

structures.name: Intermetatarsal bursa
structures.role: A cushion between the metatarsal heads; bursitis is one of four proposed causes and a differential on imaging [r3,r6]

structures.name: Metatarsal heads and plantar plates
structures.role: Form the walls of the web space; plantar plate rupture can mimic a neuroma on MRI [r6]

structures.name: Digital arteries and vasa nervorum
structures.role: Supply the nerve; arterial degeneration and ischaemia feature in histology and in the ischaemia theory [r4,r3]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
The pathomechanism is controversial, but the histological endpoint is well established as benign perineural fibrosis of a common plantar digital nerve, typically within the third intermetatarsal space [r2]. A systematic review lists neural degeneration, perineural fibrosis, arterial degeneration and oedema of the endoneurium, and describes the condition as degenerative rather than neoplastic [r4]. The lesion is not a true neuroma, although the name remains in use [r13,r3].

The relation between structure and symptoms is imperfect. Neuroma-like findings are present in up to 25% of people without symptoms, which matters when imaging is used to explain pain [r6]. A review of shoe modifications and orthoses reports that these treatments gave convincing results only in the first 4.5 months and for neuromas smaller than 5–6 mm, and suggests that larger or longer-standing lesions respond less well [r10]. Recurrent pain after surgery can be due to a stump neuroma [r12].

structures.name: Common plantar digital nerve (third web space)
structures.effect: Perineural fibrosis with thickening, degeneration and endoneurial oedema; repeated compression irritates the nerve [r2,r4]

structures.name: Deep transverse intermetatarsal ligament
structures.effect: Forms the roof of the web space; it may tether or compress the nerve when the forefoot is squeezed or the toes are extended [r3]

structures.name: Intermetatarsal bursa
structures.effect: Inflamed in some patients; bursitis is one proposed cause [r3,r6]

structures.name: Digital arteries and vasa nervorum
structures.effect: Arterial degeneration and local ischaemia are described in histology and as a proposed mechanism [r4,r3]

structures.name: Adjacent metatarsophalangeal joints
structures.effect: Synovitis or plantar plate rupture can coexist and mimic or aggravate the pain [r6]

muscles.name: Intrinsic foot muscles (interossei and lumbricals)
muscles.effect: Pain-related inhibition and avoidance of toe-off may reduce forefoot control and load sharing (clinical reasoning; not tested in the sources reviewed).

muscles.name: Gastrocnemius–soleus
muscles.effect: A tight calf can raise forefoot load during push-off (clinical reasoning); calf flexibility and strength are part of rehabilitation.

muscles.name: Peroneus longus and tibialis posterior
muscles.effect: Support the first ray and arch and shape the distribution of forefoot load (clinical reasoning).

muscles.name: Hip and trunk muscles
muscles.effect: Maintain fitness and gait mechanics during activity modification; no direct effect on the nerve.

cellular.description: Compression, traction and microtrauma, possibly with ischaemia and bursal inflammation, irritate the nerve [r3]. No staged histological timeline has been established, so the stages below are proposed.
Oedema of the endoneurium and arterial changes reduce nerve perfusion and make fibres mechanically sensitive [r4,r3].
Fibrous tissue builds up around the nerve, with neural and arterial degeneration; this is the surgical histology [r2,r4].
A thickened nerve that may be symptomatic or silent; neuroma-like findings occur in up to 25% of asymptomatic people [r6].
A stump neuroma can recur in some patients, and numbness in the toes was common after nerve excision in one long-term series [r8]. Recurrence was confirmed in the poor results of another [r7].

systems.effect: Burning, shooting pain and paraesthesia into the toes suggest neuropathic pain from an irritated sensory nerve; a thick, mechanically sensitive nerve is easily provoked by squeezing [r1].
Arterial degeneration and ischaemia of the nerve are described and may contribute [r4,r3].
Forefoot load, toe splay and footwear fit influence the squeeze on the web space; toe divergence was more common in affected feet in one case-control study [r11]; footwear fit is discussed in [r10].
Intermetatarsal bursitis and synovitis of adjacent joints can coexist and are differentials on imaging [r6,r3].
Pain on weightbearing and in footwear limits activity and quality of life [r1]; effects on mood were not examined in the sources reviewed.

timeframes.summary: No natural history studies were identified. A review of conservative care found that shoe modifications and orthoses gave convincing results only within about 4.5 months [r10]. The Cochrane review measured nonsurgical outcomes at 3 to less than 12 months and surgical outcomes at 12 months or longer [r1].

healing.description: A first-line trial. Benefit beyond about 4.5 months was not convincing in one review, and larger neuromas respond less [r10].
Trials assessed pain at three to six months after injection [r1].

healing.phase: Surgical recovery: wound and early loading
healing.description: Weeks of protected loading and wound care after neurectomy; follow the surgeon's protocol (typical clinical range).
Scar and numbness settle over months; surgical outcomes in trials were measured at 12 months or longer [r1].

milestones.label: Earliest nonsurgical outcome point in the Cochrane review
Reassess nonoperative care
milestones.note: About 4.5 months; beyond this, orthoses and shoe changes were not convincing in one review [r10]

milestones.label: Injection outcome measured
milestones.note: Three to six months in the controlled trials [r1]

timeframes.returnToSport: No validated return-to-sport (RTS) criteria were identified. Most people can continue activity in suitable footwear while symptoms allow. After neurectomy, return follows the surgeon's protocol and wound healing (clinical convention). Recovery is slow and results vary: 89.4% good results at a median of 7.1 years in one series, and 61% satisfaction at a mean of 10.5 years in a small one [r7,r8].

symptoms: Burning, shooting or electric pain in the web space that extends to the toes [r1]
A sensation of walking on a pebble or a bunched sock in the forefoot, although this feature has weak diagnostic value (sensitivity 43–53%, specificity 52%) [r1,r4]
Pain on weightbearing and walking (91% in one series) that eases with rest (81%) and with removing the shoe [r5,r4]
Numbness, tingling or paraesthesia in the adjacent sides of the toes [r4]
Pain aggravated by tight or fashionable shoes (sensitivity 73–86% across four studies) [r4]
Patient-reported clicking in the forefoot, which was specific (0.96) in one study [r4]
signs: Tenderness with direct pressure in the affected web space (100% in one retrospective series of excised neuromas) [r5]
Pain on the thumb–index finger squeeze of the web space [r4]
A palpable click and reproduction of pain when the forefoot is squeezed (Mulder's sign) in some patients [r4]
Reduced light touch or pin-prick sensation on adjacent sides of two toes in a minority [r4]
Toe divergence (the V-sign) on standing in some patients [r11]

subjective: Site and character of pain: web space between the third and fourth toes (most often), burning or shooting, radiating to the toes [r1]
Footwear relationship: aggravated by tight, narrow or high-heeled shoes and relieved by removing them; pain on walking and relief with rest [r4]
Patient-reported clicking in the forefoot (specificity 0.96 in one study) [r4]
Duration and trial of treatment so far: footwear changes, orthoses, injections; longer duration and larger neuromas respond less to orthoses [r10]
Previous forefoot surgery or neurectomy (stump neuroma) and other foot conditions [r12]
Red flags and mimics: night pain, systemic symptoms, diabetes or neuropathy, back pain with leg symptoms, joint swelling
observation: Toe alignment and splay (the V-sign) when standing
Forefoot shape, hallux valgus, lesser toe deformity and callosities
palpation: Web space between the metatarsal heads, from the plantar surface, with the toes slightly extended: localised tenderness [r5,r4]
Metatarsal heads and metatarsophalangeal joints (synovitis, plantar plate tear) [r6]
Intermetatarsal bursa and dorsal web space
Compare the second to fourth web spaces and both feet
rangeOfMotion: Metatarsophalangeal dorsiflexion and plantarflexion: toe extension may provoke symptoms
Ankle dorsiflexion (calf tightness raises forefoot load; clinical reasoning)
Great toe motion and first ray mobility
Lesser toe stability (vertical drawer) to exclude plantar plate injury
strength: Intrinsic foot strength: short-foot and toe flexion
Calf endurance: single-leg heel raise tolerance
Peroneus longus and first ray control
neuro: Light touch and pin-prick sensation on the adjacent sides of the toes of the affected web space (the sensitivity of a sensory deficit was only about 25–50% in the studies reviewed) [r4]
Tinel-type percussion over the web space and the tarsal tunnel to exclude proximal nerve involvement
Lower limb neurological screen (reflexes, power, sensation) to exclude radiculopathy and peripheral neuropathy
functional: Gait barefoot and in usual footwear
Sport and footwear demands, for example dance en pointe and running shoes

specialTests.name: Modified web space tenderness test (thumb–index finger squeeze test)
specialTests.purpose: Rule out a Morton's neuroma when negative
specialTests.procedure: Place the pad of the thumb on the plantar web space and the index finger on the dorsal web space, and apply firm pressure without squeezing the forefoot laterally. Compare spaces and sides [r4].
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of the web space pain or tenderness. In one prospective cohort of 40 patients, sensitivity was 0.96 and the negative likelihood ratio 0.04, but only one participant lacked a neuroma, so specificity could not be estimated. Other web space tenderness tests had sensitivity of 57–95% and very weak likelihood ratios [r4].

specialTests.name: Mulder's click test
specialTests.purpose: Reproduce the click and pain from the thickened nerve and bursa
specialTests.procedure: Squeeze the forefoot from the sides so that the metatarsal heads are pushed together while pressing on the plantar web space with the other thumb [r4].
specialTests.positive: A palpable or audible click, often with pain, numbness or tingling. Across three studies, sensitivity ranged from 29% to 94% and specificity from 17% to 100%; the one reported positive likelihood ratio was 2.19, which is weak evidence [r4]. In a retrospective series of excised neuromas, it was the most sensitive clinical sign, and clinical assessment overall had sensitivity of 98% (42/43) [r5].

specialTests.name: Foot (metatarsal) squeeze test
specialTests.purpose: Provoke the web space pain by transverse compression
specialTests.procedure: Compress the forefoot transversely across the metatarsal heads with the whole hand and ask about pain in the web space [r4].
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of the forefoot pain. Sensitivity ranged from 0% to 88% and specificity from 0% to 78% across studies, with no study showing clinical usefulness, so this test cannot rule a neuroma in or out [r4].

specialTests.name: Sensory testing of the adjacent toe sides
specialTests.purpose: Look for a sensory deficit in the distribution of the nerve
specialTests.procedure: Test light touch and pin-prick on the facing sides of the two affected toes and compare with the neighbouring toes and the other foot [r4].
specialTests.positive: A deficit in the distribution. Sensitivity was low in studies (25% for light touch or pin-prick in one study and 49% for toe-tip sensation in another), so a normal result does not exclude a neuroma [r4].

specialTests.name: Lesser MTP vertical drawer and joint palpation
specialTests.purpose: Exclude plantar plate injury and synovitis, which mimic a neuroma
specialTests.procedure: Stabilise the metatarsal head and apply dorsal and plantar force to the proximal phalanx, then palpate the joint line and compare with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Pain, laxity or joint-line tenderness points to a plantar plate or joint cause rather than a neuroma [r6]. No accuracy data were identified in the sources reviewed.

clinicalRules.name: Clinical diagnosis first; imaging for unclear or multiple-space presentations
clinicalRules.description: In a retrospective series, clinical assessment had 98% sensitivity (42/43) and the authors found no absolute requirement for imaging; the two indications they gave were an unclear clinical assessment and more than one affected web space [r5]. The accuracy of clinical diagnosis varies between 58% and 93% across studies, and UK primary care guidance advises that further investigation is generally unnecessary [r4].

clinicalRules.name: Interpret imaging against the symptoms
clinicalRules.description: Neuroma-like findings are present in up to 25% of asymptomatic people, so a lesion on imaging does not prove the web space is the pain source [r6].

clinicalRules.name: Reassess nonoperative care at about 4.5 months
clinicalRules.description: Orthoses and shoe modifications gave convincing results only within about 4.5 months, and less in neuromas larger than 5–6 mm; beyond that, consider injection or surgical referral [r10].

outcomeMeasures.name: Visual analogue scale (VAS) pain, 0–100 mm
outcomeMeasures.use: The primary outcome in the Cochrane review and trials [r1]

outcomeMeasures.name: AOFAS Lesser Toe Metatarsophalangeal-Interphalangeal Scale and Manchester Foot Pain and Disability Schedule (MFPDS)
Manchester-Oxford Foot Questionnaire (MOXFQ) and EQ-5D
outcomeMeasures.use: Foot-specific function and health-related quality of life [r1]

outcomeMeasures.name: Self-reported foot and ankle score (SEFAS) and a 3-grade patient satisfaction scale
outcomeMeasures.use: Used after neurectomy in observational series [r12,r7]

imaging.indication: To exclude bony causes (stress fracture, arthritis, deformity); not diagnostic for neuroma
imaging.findings: The 'Vulcan salute' (V-sign, divergence of the toes) was present in 30 of 100 patients with MRI-proven neuroma and 3 of 100 controls (sensitivity 30%, specificity 97%), so it is specific but insensitive [r11].

imaging.indication: First-choice imaging when the clinical picture is unclear or more than one web space is affected; also guides injection [r5,r2]
imaging.findings: Sensitivity was 90% (28/31) in one series; ultrasound is highly accurate but depends on the operator and technique [r5,r2]. Ultrasound-guided steroid injection probably reduces pain more than non-guided injection [r1].

imaging.indication: Unclear diagnosis, suspected multiple lesions, suspected mimics or before surgery [r6,r5]
imaging.findings: Sensitivity was 88% (14/16) in one series [r5]. MRI helps to exclude plantar plate rupture, bursitis, rheumatoid or gouty nodules and tenosynovial giant cell tumour, but up to 25% of asymptomatic people have similar findings [r6].

differentials.name: Metatarsophalangeal joint synovitis or plantar plate tear
differentials.distinguishing: Pain and swelling at the MTP joint, a positive vertical drawer and pain on joint palpation; a plantar plate rupture can produce a neuroma-like mass on MRI [r6].

differentials.name: Metatarsal stress fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Focal bony tenderness at the metatarsal neck or shaft, pain with hopping and a stress response on MRI, rather than web space nerve pain.

differentials.name: Intermetatarsal bursitis
differentials.distinguishing: Swelling and tenderness in the web space without nerve symptoms; the two can coexist and are hard to separate clinically and on imaging [r6,r3].

differentials.name: Tarsal tunnel syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Burning in the sole with Tinel's sign behind the medial malleolus and symptoms across the sole beyond a single web space.

differentials.name: Peripheral neuropathy or lumbosacral radiculopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Bilateral or stocking distribution symptoms, back or leg pain, reflex or power changes. Check systemic causes such as diabetes.

differentials.name: Freiberg's disease or osteochondritis of the metatarsal head
differentials.distinguishing: Metatarsal head pain and joint stiffness, often in adolescents, with radiographic collapse of the head.

differentials.name: Rheumatoid or gouty nodules, tenosynovial giant cell tumour
differentials.distinguishing: A soft-tissue mass with systemic features or joint involvement; MRI helps to distinguish [r6].

differentials.name: Plantar fat pad atrophy or forefoot overload metatarsalgia
differentials.distinguishing: Diffuse plantar forefoot pain under the metatarsal heads without web space or digital nerve features.

redFlags: Constant or night pain, an enlarging or hard mass, weight loss, or a history of cancer: consider tumour or another structural cause and refer for imaging and specialist assessment.
A hot, red, swollen forefoot or toe with fever, or an open wound or ulcer: suspect infection or an inflammatory arthropathy and arrange urgent medical review.

Bilateral, stocking-distribution or progressive numbness, or associated back pain, weakness or reflex change: suspect polyneuropathy or radiculopathy and refer for neurological or medical review [r4].
Diabetes, peripheral vascular disease or loss of protective sensation: do not attribute forefoot pain to a neuroma without review, and avoid injections or surgery without specialist input.
Symptoms not improved after a structured nonoperative trial of about 4.5 months, or severe pain limiting walking: refer for injection or surgical review [r10].

After corticosteroid injection: skin atrophy, depigmentation or fat pad atrophy (reported in 2.6–3.9% each in trials); after surgery: recurrent pain (stump neuroma), wound infection, persistent numbness or calf pain: arrange review [r1,r12].

management.principles: Make the diagnosis clinically, with imaging when the picture is unclear, and match treatment to symptoms and goals [r5,r4]. The usual sequence is footwear and orthoses, then injection, then surgery [r3,r10]. The evidence is thin: the Cochrane review found only six small randomised trials (373 participants) with some concerns about bias in most outcomes, and it found no trial comparing surgery with nonoperative care [r1]. Corticosteroid added to local anaesthetic may make little or no difference to pain or function at three to six months, whereas ultrasound-guided injection probably reduces pain and improves function compared with non-guided injection [r1]. Reviews that include observational studies are more positive about steroid, alcohol, capsaicin, hyaluronic acid and radiofrequency treatments, but they cannot separate treatment effect from natural variation [r9,r14]. Surgery gives good results in many patients, but numbness is common and a minority have recurrent pain [r7,r8]. Discuss the uncertainty with the patient and agree on a time limit for each step.

medical.name: Corticosteroid plus local anaesthetic injection
medical.description: In two RCTs (157 participants), corticosteroid plus local anaesthetic versus local anaesthetic alone made little to no difference to pain at 3–6 months (MD –6.31 mm on a 100 mm VAS, 95% CI –14.23 to 1.61; low-certainty evidence) or to function. Adverse events were reported with steroid: mild skin atrophy (3.9%), hypopigmentation (3.9%) and plantar fat pad atrophy (2.6%), none with local anaesthetic alone, although the evidence was very uncertain [r1]. Observational reviews report high efficacy for steroid injection [r9]; they are not controlled.

medical.name: Ultrasound-guided injection (rather than non-guided)
medical.description: In two RCTs (116 feet), ultrasound-guided corticosteroid plus local anaesthetic probably reduced pain compared with non-guided injection (MD –15.01 mm, 95% CI –27.88 to –2.14; moderate-certainty evidence) and probably improved function, and may have increased satisfaction (risk ratio 1.71). Depigmentation or fat atrophy occurred in 4.9% versus 12.7%, a difference the review rated low-certainty [r1].

medical.name: Local anaesthetic injection alone
medical.description: Local anaesthetic alone was the comparator in two RCTs; no adverse events were observed, and it was not clearly worse than steroid plus anaesthetic at 3–6 months [r1].

medical.name: Other injections: alcohol (sclerosant), capsaicin, hyaluronic acid
medical.description: A review of 12 studies (6 RCTs and 6 observational studies, 1,438 patients) reported a 51.8% VAS reduction with capsaicin and a high level of efficacy with steroid; alcohol and hyaluronic acid were well tolerated but need more research, and there were no serious adverse events [r9]. These data include observational studies and are less certain than the controlled trials.

medical.name: Radiofrequency ablation
medical.description: A meta-analysis of 8 studies (237 patients; trials, cohorts and case series) found significant pain reduction; at final follow-up 47.57% had complete pain relief and 16.40% no benefit. Settings of 85°C or above and three or fewer cycles gave greater relief, and complications were 2.1% [r14].

medical.name: Neurectomy (nerve excision), plantar or dorsal approach
medical.description: Indicated when nonsurgical treatment fails [r7]. In 160 patients followed for a median of 7.1 years after a plantar approach, 89.4% had a good result, 6.9% fair and 3.8% poor; the six poor results had a confirmed recurrent neuroma [r7]. In a small series of 13 followed for more than 10 years, satisfaction was 61% and 11 had numbness, with 2 reporting disability from severe numbness [r8]. A review cites a success rate of 74% for primary excision [r12]. The Cochrane review found low-certainty evidence of little or no difference in satisfaction between plantar and dorsal approaches (RR 1.06) in one study. In a meta-analysis, scar tenderness was more common after the plantar approach (16.7% versus 6.2%) and reoperation rates were similar (5.3% versus 6.1%) [r1,r15]. The Cochrane review included no RCT of surgery versus nonoperative care.

medical.name: Nerve decompression (neurolysis), with or without transposition
medical.description: A systematic review of 22 studies of operations other than neurectomy found lower postoperative neurogenic symptoms with neurolysis than with neurectomy, but whether these procedures are superior remains unclear; minimally invasive ligament release and metatarsal osteotomy were inconclusive. If the nerve is cut, embedding the end in muscle was recommended [r16].

physio.name: Education and footwear modification
physio.description: Advise shoes that are long, comfortable, broad in the toe box, flat-heeled and with a sole that is thick enough and not excessively flexible; this is the first step in early stages and aims to limit nerve compression [r10].

physio.name: Orthoses with a metatarsal pad or retrocapital bar
physio.description: An insole with medial arch support and a retrocapital bar or pad just proximal to the metatarsal heads displaces the pressure sites. Beyond about 4.5 months and in neuromas larger than 5–6 mm, results were not convincing, and orthoses seemed palliative rather than curative [r10]. The review draws on observational studies; no controlled trial was identified.

physio.name: Load management and activity modification
physio.description: Reduce repeated forefoot loading with the toes extended (high heels, hill running, repeated relevé, kneeling and squatting) while symptoms settle (clinical convention; no trial identified).

physio.name: Calf, intrinsic foot and hip strengthening and calf flexibility
physio.description: Improve load sharing across the foot and reduce peak forefoot load (clinical reasoning; no trial of exercise for Morton's neuroma was identified).

physio.name: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy
physio.description: A systematic review of foot and ankle disorders stated that the evidence indicated ESWT could help manage Morton's neuroma, but it said further well-designed studies were warranted [r17]. No Morton's neuroma trial was verified here.

physio.name: Manual therapy, neural mobilisation and taping or toe spacers
physio.description: Used clinically to settle symptoms and unload the web space. No trial for Morton's neuroma was identified (clinical convention).

physio.name: Continued wear of narrow, high-heeled or tight footwear
physio.description: Footwear that squeezes the forefoot is the factor most often blamed, and shoe changes are the first step in treatment [r10].

physio.name: Repeated corticosteroid injections without a response to the first
physio.description: The Cochrane review found little or no added benefit of steroid over anaesthetic, with skin atrophy, hypopigmentation and fat pad atrophy reported (very-low-certainty evidence) [r1].

education: Morton's neuroma is a thickening and scarring (fibrosis) of a nerve between the toes. It is not a tumour and it is not cancer.
Wide-toed, flat shoes and a metatarsal pad often help at first. If there is no improvement in about four to five months, injections or surgery can be discussed.

Injections can help some people, but the best-quality trials show that adding steroid to local anaesthetic gives little extra benefit, and an injection guided by ultrasound probably works better than one given without guidance.
Surgery to remove the nerve works well for many people but leaves numbness in the toes, and a small number get recurrent pain.
An abnormal scan does not always mean the nerve is the cause: up to one in four people without symptoms have a similar finding.
Keep active within pain limits and tell your clinician about night pain, a fever or numbness spreading up the foot or leg.

rehab.overview: Rehabilitation for Morton's neuroma is conservative and criteria-based. It aims to unload the web space, restore foot and calf function, and return the person to activity in suitable footwear. No controlled trial of an exercise program was identified, so the stages below follow clinical reasoning, and the main sourced element is footwear and orthosis change, with benefit seen mainly in the first 4.5 months [r10]. If symptoms do not improve, the next steps are injection or surgical review [r1]. After a neurectomy or injection, follow the clinician's protocol. Dosages are typical clinical ranges, not prescriptions from a single source.

stages.name: Unload & settle
goals: Reduce web space compression and pain
Educate on the condition and the plan
precautions: Avoid narrow, tight or high-heeled shoes and activities that provoke burning pain
Stop and review for night pain, spreading numbness or fever
After injection, rest from impact for the days advised by the clinician

exercises.name: Seated ankle range of motion
exercises.cues: Slow and pain-free; keep the toes relaxed

exercises.name: Calf stretch (gastrocnemius and soleus)
exercises.cues: Heel down and foot straight; stop before forefoot pain

exercises.name: Metatarsal pad or retrocapital bar fit and walking program
exercises.dosage: Wear daily; walk 15–20 min on a flat, soft surface
exercises.cues: The pad sits just behind the metatarsal heads, not under them

exercises.name: Double-leg glute bridge
exercises.cues: Weight through the heels; keep the forefoot relaxed

exercises.name: Cycling or swimming with forefoot offloading
exercises.cues: Place the foot with the pedal under the arch rather than the ball of the foot where possible

progressionCriteria: Resting and walking pain reduced by at least a third compared with baseline (clinical convention)
Suitable footwear and orthoses in daily use
Night pain absent and no new numbness

stages.name: Restore foot function
goals: Restore intrinsic foot and calf strength
precautions: Keep burning pain at or below 3/10 during and after exercise (clinical convention)
Avoid sustained toe extension on tiptoe at first
Review at about 4.5 months if there is no benefit [r10]

exercises.name: Short-foot (arch) activation, seated then standing
exercises.cues: Shorten the foot without curling the toes or clawing

exercises.name: Seated calf raise
exercises.cues: Press through the whole forefoot, not only the toes

exercises.name: Toe spreading and toe-flexion strengthening
exercises.cues: Spread the toes gently without pinching the web space

exercises.name: Single-leg balance in supportive footwear
exercises.cues: Soft knee and quiet trunk

exercises.name: Walking program in broad-toed shoes
exercises.cues: Heel-to-toe roll with an even push-off

progressionCriteria: Walks 30 min with pain at or below 3/10 and settling the next day

stages.name: Progressive loading
goals: Build calf and forefoot load capacity
Return to stairs, step-ups and brisk walking
precautions: Progress in small steps; stop if burning pain returns for more than 24 h
Use a rocker sole or stiff insole if toe-off provokes pain

exercises.name: Double-leg calf raise, then single-leg
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10–12 building to single-leg 3 × 8–12, every second day
exercises.cues: Even load across the metatarsal heads and avoid rolling outwards

exercises.name: Single-leg calf raise
exercises.dosage: 3 × 8–12, 3 s up and 3 s down, every second day
exercises.cues: Full range with the weight over the first and second toes

exercises.name: Step-up and controlled step-down
exercises.cues: Keep the pelvis level and the knee over the second toe

exercises.name: Brisk walking and treadmill incline walking
exercises.cues: Smooth push-off in suitable shoes

exercises.name: Single-leg balance with perturbation
exercises.cues: Keep the arch active and the toes long

progressionCriteria: Single-leg calf raise × 15 with pain at or below 2/10
Brisk walking 40 min without a flare
Pain at or below 2/10 in activity footwear

stages.name: Return to impact & sport
stages.timeframe: Weeks 10–16+ (criteria-based; review the plan at about 4.5 months if no benefit [r10])
goals: Return to running, jumping and sport-specific work
Plan long-term footwear and load management
Decide on injection or surgery if there is no benefit
precautions: Add volume and intensity in steps and keep the footwear plan
Do not return to high-forefoot-load sport while burning pain persists
Stop and refer if night pain, spreading numbness or signs of infection appear

exercises.name: Walk–run program
exercises.dosage: 1 min run / 2 min walk for 20 min, 3 times a week, adding running every 1–2 sessions (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Midfoot landing with an even push-off

exercises.name: Single-leg hop in place, forward and lateral
exercises.cues: Soft landing; stop if burning pain returns

exercises.name: Jump landing and rebound drills
exercises.cues: Land on the whole foot with hips and knees bent

exercises.name: Dancers: graded relevé progression
exercises.dosage: Double-leg relevé 3 × 10, then demi-pointe and single-leg over 4–8 weeks (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Weight over the first and second toes; avoid sinking into the forefoot

exercises.name: Sport-specific drills and graded training
exercises.dosage: Partial then full training over 2–3 weeks
exercises.cues: Monitor burning pain and numbness and adjust footwear

progressionCriteria: Full training for at least 2 weeks with pain at or below 1/10 and no next-day flare
Hop and calf-raise capacity at or above 90% of the other side (clinical convention)
Suitable footwear and orthosis plan in place
If symptoms persist, injection or surgical review agreed with the patient

criteria: No validated return-to-sport (RTS) criteria were identified for Morton's neuroma; the criteria below reflect clinical convention
Walking and jogging with forefoot pain at or below 2/10 in activity footwear, settled by the next day
No night pain, spreading numbness or new neurological signs
Calf and hop performance at or above about 90% of the other side (clinical convention)
Dancers: pain-free relevé and demi-pointe in the appropriate footwear before returning to full class
A footwear, orthosis and load plan agreed with the athlete; after surgery, the surgeon's clearance
tests: Web space palpation and the thumb–index finger squeeze test
Walking and jogging tolerance with pain rating
Single-leg heel raise repetitions and pain
Single-leg hop tests with pain rating
Weekly training volume and next-day symptom log

prognosis: Outcomes vary and the evidence is limited. Orthoses and shoe changes gave convincing results only within about 4.5 months and in neuromas smaller than 5–6 mm in one review [r10]. In the Cochrane review, steroid added to local anaesthetic made little difference to pain, and the few trials were small [r1]. Observational reviews report pain relief after injection and radiofrequency ablation, with 47.57% complete pain relief and 16.40% no benefit after radiofrequency [r9,r14]. After plantar-approach neurectomy, 89.4% of 160 patients had a good result at a median of 7.1 years, and the poor results had a confirmed recurrence [r7]. A smaller series found 61% satisfaction at a mean of 10.5 years, with numbness in 11 of 13, and concluded that long-term results were slightly worse than short- and mid-term results [r8]. Excision of a primary neuroma has a reported success rate of 74%, and revision of recurrent neuromas through a dorsal approach gave excellent scores in 17 of 23 patients [r12]. Because there is no randomised comparison of surgery with nonoperative care, outcomes cannot be compared directly [r1].
prevention: No prevention trial was identified. A review of conservative care suggests that shoes should be sufficiently long, comfortable, broad in the toe box and flat-heeled, with a sufficiently thick sole that is not excessively flexible, to help prevent or delay the condition [r10].
Limit prolonged high-heeled or narrow footwear and repeated forefoot loading with the toes extended (clinical observation).
Maintain calf flexibility and foot strength, and review footwear when forefoot symptoms first appear (clinical observation).
Treat early symptoms promptly with footwear and orthosis changes, because results were better in the first 4.5 months and in smaller neuromas [r10].
Review forefoot overload from deformities such as hallux valgus or hammer toes (clinical observation).
clinicalPearls: Diagnose clinically. Patient-reported clicking was the only strong rule-in feature (specificity 0.96, LR+ 13.14, one low-risk study), and a negative modified web space tenderness test (thumb–index finger squeeze) helped to rule it out (LR– 0.04, one study) [r4].
Do not rely on the classic descriptors: a pebble in the shoe had sensitivity 43–53% and specificity 52%, and burning had 54–57% and 48%, so neither helps much [r4].
Mulder's click is popular but unreliable: sensitivity 29–94%, specificity 17–100% and a weak likelihood ratio, so a negative test does not exclude a neuroma [r4].
Imaging can mislead: neuroma-like findings are present in up to 25% of asymptomatic people. Match the lesion to the symptoms before surgery [r6].
If an injection is chosen, use ultrasound guidance: it probably reduces pain more than non-guided injection, whereas steroid added to anaesthetic gave little extra benefit in two trials [r1].

Counsel before surgery: numbness is common (11 of 13 at more than 10 years in one series), recurrence occurs, and the plantar approach had more scar tenderness than the dorsal approach (16.7% versus 6.2%) [r8,r15].

forces.label: Forefoot load with the toes extended

captions.text: A dancer repeats a movement that loads the forefoot with the toes extended.
In relevé, the whole body weight is carried on the metatarsal heads.
Running, high heels and squatting load the forefoot in a similar way.
Narrow or tight shoes squeeze the metatarsal heads together.
Over months, the nerve between the toes is repeatedly compressed. There is no single injury.
Zooming into the forefoot, viewed from above (dorsal view).
A common plantar digital nerve runs between the metatarsal heads in each web space.
It passes beneath the deep transverse metatarsal ligament, which forms the roof of the space.
When the forefoot is squeezed or the toes are extended, the nerve is compressed against the ligament.
The nerve becomes irritated, and fires pain signals.
Over time it thickens with scar tissue. This is perineural fibrosis, not a true tumour.
The third web space is the most common site, with burning pain to the toes and a pebble feeling.
Squeezing the forefoot can sometimes produce a click, although the sign is not very accurate.
Scans can show a thickened nerve even in people with no symptoms.
Healthy nerve: insulated fibres with a good blood supply. Schematic nerve model.
Compression: repeated squeezing narrows the space around the nerve.
Ischaemia: compressed vessels reduce the nerve's blood supply.
Demyelination: the insulating sheath thins and signals misfire.
Axonal injury: in long-standing cases, fibres degenerate. The perineural scar of Morton's neuroma is not drawn here.
